title: Layers, encapsulation and devices
subtitle: A network is a stack of small promises: each layer uses the one below and offers a simpler service to the one above.

why.title: Why layers
why.body:
Sending a web page across the world involves electrical signals, error checking, finding a route, making delivery reliable and speaking HTTP. Nobody builds that as one program. A layered architecture splits the job: each layer talks to the same layer on the other machine through a protocol, and uses only the service of the layer beneath it. Layers can be replaced independently — Wi-Fi for Ethernet — without touching the layers above.

The OSI model has seven layers (physical, data link, network, transport, session, presentation, application); the TCP/IP model that the Internet actually uses has four: link, internet, transport, application.

encap.title: Encapsulation
encap.body: Going down the stack each layer adds its own header (the data link layer also a trailer) around what it was given. The application data becomes a TCP segment, then an IP packet, then an Ethernet frame, then bits. The receiver peels the headers off in reverse. Each header carries exactly what that layer needs: ports, IP addresses, MAC addresses.
encap.steps: A 1000-byte application message goes through TCP (20-byte header), IP (20) and Ethernet (14 + 4 trailer). Frame size = 1000 + 20 + 20 + 14 + 4. Overhead fraction.

types.title: Networks and topologies
types.body: A LAN covers a building, a MAN a city, a WAN a country or more. Topologies: bus (one shared cable), star (all to a central switch — the modern LAN), ring, mesh (many links, resilient). In a client–server network servers provide services; in peer-to-peer every host is both.

devices.title: Devices by layer
devices.body: A repeater/hub regenerates bits (layer 1, floods every port, one collision domain). A bridge/switch forwards frames by MAC address (layer 2), learning which address lives on which port. A router forwards packets between networks by IP address (layer 3). A gateway translates between different protocol stacks, often at the application layer.

addr.title: Addressing at each layer
addr.body: Four kinds of address work together: a port picks the process (transport), an IP address picks the host across networks (network), a MAC address picks the interface on one link (data link), and a name such as example.com is turned into an IP by DNS (application). Along a route the IP addresses stay the same end to end while the MAC addresses change at every hop.

summary.title: Summary
summary.body:
• Layers hide complexity; each talks to its peer via a protocol.
  • Going down, headers are added; going up, removed.
  • Hub → switch → router see layers 1 → 2 → 3.
